title: Ordination
hookLine: hands laid on, and prayer for the Spirit

cards: Nobody in the church moves. At the front, a person in a plain white robe kneels on the stone floor, head bowed. The bishop places both hands on that head.
Then, one after another, others come and add their hands, on the head, on the shoulders, until a small crowd of palms rests on one person. The silence stretches.
Then a prayer goes up, asking the Holy Spirit to come on the one kneeling there. When the person stands, the robe is the same. For the church, something has changed.

teach.b: Ordination is how a church sets someone apart for ministry, and at its center is a very old gesture: hands laid on, with prayer. It runs all through Acts. First, helpers in Jerusalem.
The apostles need people to look after the widows' daily food, and the church chooses some: "when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them." Prayer first, then hands. Second, a sending.
In Antioch, the church is worshipping and fasting, and the Holy Spirit says, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them."
Then, "when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away." Barnabas and Saul are already among that church's teachers. The hands don't keep them; they send them off.
Third, a gift that needs tending. Paul tells Timothy: "Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery."
And in a second letter: "stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands." Stir it up, the way you'd stir a fire burning low. Fourth, where churches differ.
Catholics and Orthodox call holy orders a sacrament: bishops ordain deacons, priests and other bishops, and they see a line of laid-on hands reaching back to the apostles. Anglicans keep bishops too.
Other Protestant churches ordain ministers with hands laid on by other ministers or elders. Quakers ordain no one. Churches also differ on who may be ordained.
Where they do ordain, hands and prayer tend to be at the center, as in Acts.

how: In Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, a bishop ordains deacons, priests and bishops by laying on hands with prayer; other Protestant churches ordain ministers with the laying on of hands by other ministers or elders; Quakers do not ordain.

games.q: you're the church in Antioch, fasting and worshipping. the Holy Spirit says: "separate me Barnabas and Saul." they're two of your own teachers. what do you do?
o: hold a vote on whether to let them go.
fast, pray, lay your hands on them, and send them away.
keep them home, where they're needed most.
games.why: "when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away." the hands don't keep them. they send them.

practice: Bring to mind your pastor, priest or minister, or, if you don't have one, someone who has cared for your spirit another way: a teacher, a grandparent, a friend who listens. Picture your hand resting lightly on their shoulder.
If you pray, ask God to stir up the gift in them; if you don't, simply wish them strength for the work.

wordCard.voice: Ordination. A church setting someone apart for ministry, with hands and prayer for the Spirit, then sending them out.

orig.note: Greek: the laying on of the hands, the phrase Paul uses to Timothy in 1 Timothy 4:14.
